title: Bucatini all'Amatriciana
subtitle: bucatini with guanciale, tomato and pecorino
excerpt: Bucatini all'amatriciana is a Roman pasta of thick hollow spaghetti coated in a sharp tomato sauce made from rendered guanciale, dried chilli and white wine, finished with grated parmesan. The sauce is quick to make but requires guanciale, the cured pork cheek that gives amatriciana its particular flavour. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Amatriciana takes its name from Amatrice, a town in the Lazio mountains, where it originated as a shepherds' dish without tomatoes. Tomatoes were added when the dish moved to Rome in the nineteenth century and became one of the four canonical Roman pasta dishes alongside cacio e pepe, carbonara and gricia. Amatrice still holds a festival in its honour each August.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian cured pork cheek, fattier and more intensely flavoured than pancetta, used in Roman pasta dishes including carbonara and amatriciana.
A Roman pasta sauce of guanciale, tomatoes and pecorino, originating in the town of Amatrice in the Lazio mountains.

content.text: rendered slowly in a dry pan until the fat has melted and the meat is crisp at the edges. White wine deglazes the pan, then tomatoes go in and reduce to a thick, clinging sauce. The technique of rendering the guanciale first rather than frying it quickly is what sets the flavour base for everything else. Serves 4.
Traditionally this dish uses pecorino romano, but parmesan is used here as a practical substitute with a similar effect. If you can find pecorino, use it.

items.prepNote: cut into 1cm cubes or thick strips

content.text: Put the guanciale in a cold frying pan with the olive oil. Set over medium-low heat and cook slowly for 8 to 10 minutes until the fat has rendered and the meat is starting to crisp at the edges. Do not rush this.
Add the chilli flakes and cook for 30 seconds. Pour in the white wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes until mostly evaporated.
Add the tinned tomatoes and break them up. Season to taste. Simmer over medium heat for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and slightly reduced.
Meanwhile, cook the bucatini in a large pan of boiling water according to packet instructions. Reserve a mug of pasta water before draining.

Add the drained pasta to the sauce and toss over low heat for 1 minute, adding a splash of pasta water to loosen if needed. Remove from the heat and stir in half the parmesan. Serve with the remaining cheese on top.

attrs.symptom: Guanciale is chewy rather than crisp at the edges
attrs.cause: The heat was too high and the fat did not have time to render properly
attrs.fix: Start in a cold pan on medium-low heat. The fat needs time to melt out slowly before the meat can crisp

attrs.symptom: Sauce is too acidic and sharp
attrs.cause: The tinned tomatoes were high-acid or the sauce did not reduce long enough
attrs.fix: Simmer for the full 15 minutes. The reduction mellows the acidity. A tiny pinch of caster sugar can help if it still tastes sharp

attrs.symptom: Pasta is clumping before it goes into the sauce
attrs.cause: It was drained too early and left sitting without any fat or water to keep it loose
attrs.fix: Drain the pasta while the sauce is in the pan ready and move it straight across. Reserve pasta water and add a splash if it starts to stick

content.text: Amatriciana is one of Rome's four canonical pasta dishes, eaten across the city in trattorias and homes. It originates in Amatrice in the Lazio hills, where the original version had no tomatoes. Romans adopted it and added the tomato sauce in the nineteenth century. Debates about the correct recipe, particularly whether onion belongs in it, are ongoing and strongly held.
